nature-gov-010.title: The Sustainable Development Goals: 17 goals for 2030
nature-gov-010.text: On 25 September 2015, the 193 countries of the UN General Assembly adopted a plan with a bold title: "Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development." At its heart sit the Sustainable Development Goals, or SDGs. There are 17 goals with 169 measurable targets, and they tie together the environmental, social and economic sides of sustainable development. Each goal usually has eight to 12 targets, and each target has one to four indicators, about 1.5 on average. The goals are universal and time-bound, but they bind no one legally. Three focus on the environment: SDG 13 on climate, SDG 14 on oceans and SDG 15 on land. There is no single goal for the planet as a whole. The SDGs replaced the Millennium Development Goals, which ended in 2015. Critics note the new list is much longer than the eight goals it replaced. Progress is slow. A 2024 UN report found only 17% of targets on track. The 2025 report said 35% were on track or making moderate progress, while 18% were going backward. Rising inequality, climate change and biodiversity loss threaten the rest, and the COVID-19 pandemic slowed things further.

nature-gov-015.title: The Convention on Biological Diversity
nature-gov-015.text: Of all the UN's member states, only the United States has not ratified it, citing sovereignty and economic interests. The Convention on Biological Diversity, informally the Biodiversity Convention, is a treaty for conserving the variety of life on Earth. It has three main goals. Conserve biodiversity. Use its parts sustainably. Share fairly the benefits that come from the genes of living things, a topic covered in {{ref:nature-gov-046}}. The idea took shape at a UNEP expert working group in November 1988. The treaty opened for signature at the 1992 summit in Rio de Janeiro on 5 June 1992 and entered into force on 29 December 1993. As of 2016 it had 196 parties. Its secretariat sits in Montreal under UNEP. Two extra agreements hang from it, one on biosafety and one on sharing benefits, described in {{ref:nature-gov-044}} and {{ref:nature-gov-036}}. It regulates access to genes and traditional knowledge, which requires the prior informed consent of the country providing them. Its Strategic Plan for Biodiversity 2011–2020 held a set of targets, described in {{ref:nature-gov-017}}, later followed by the post-2020 Global Biodiversity Framework.

nature-gov-038.title: Protected areas: fencing off nature's value
nature-gov-038.text: Over 2000 years ago, royal decrees in India set certain areas apart. Protecting places is old. A protected area is a place guarded for its natural or cultural value, where human use of resources is limited. The IUCN, the world conservation body, defines it more precisely. It is a clearly bounded space managed, by law or other means, to conserve nature and its services long term. Those services are a big part of the point. Protecting biodiversity also protects water, fuel, carbon storage and climate regulation. Under Article 8 of the Biodiversity Convention, parties agreed to build systems of protected areas. As of 2016, over 161,000 of them covered about 17 percent of the world's land, not counting Antarctica. At sea, 14,688 marine protected areas cover about 10.2% of coastal and marine areas and 4.12% of the global ocean. Protection has a cost for some people. New restrictions can displace local communities. That sours relations with conservationists and sometimes drives poaching.

nature-gov-046.title: Genetic resources: who owns life's code?
nature-gov-046.text: A seed bank is a library of genes. Germplasm, genetic material kept for breeding, preservation and research, is one example. Genetic resources are genetic material from plants, animals, microbes or other sources with actual or potential value. The Biodiversity Convention in 1992 named them one of the three levels of biodiversity. Earlier agreements treated them as the common heritage of humankind, open to all. Developing countries objected. Their resources were taken without payment and turned into products in industrialized nations. The convention changed the rule, giving each state sovereign rights over the genetic resources on its territory.

nature-gov-052.title: UNCLOS: the treaty that governs the oceans
nature-gov-052.text: Negotiations ran from 1973 to 1982 at the third UN Conference on the Law of the Sea. The result, the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, or UNCLOS, sets the legal framework for all marine and maritime activities. It entered into force on 16 November 1994. It replaced the 17th-century idea of freedom of the seas, under which waters beyond a narrow coastal belt belonged to no nation. It sets zones measured from a coastal baseline, including exclusive economic zones reaching 200 nautical miles. Part XI created the International Seabed Authority to license seabed mining and share royalties. Part XII obliges all states to cooperate in protecting the marine environment. It has 172 parties, and the United States has signed but not ratified it. It had a gap: no framework for biodiversity beyond national waters. A 2023 treaty, described in {{ref:nature-gov-049}}, was added to fill it.

nature-gov-027.title: SDG 14: life below water
nature-gov-027.text: Oceans cover over 70% of Earth's surface. Yet from 2013 to 2021, only 1.1% of national research budgets went to ocean science. Sustainable Development Goal 14, "Life below water," aims to conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources. Its ten targets cover pollution, ecosystem protection, acidification, sustainable fishing and conserving coastal areas. Target 14.5 aimed to protect at least 10 per cent of coastal and marine areas by 2020. Target 14.4 is measured by the share of fish stocks within biologically sustainable levels. The water itself is changing. Ocean pH now averages 8.1, about 30% more acidic than before industrialization. Sustainable fisheries made up roughly 0.1 per cent of global GDP in 2017. The World Economic Forum estimates that reaching the goal needs US$175 billion a year in ocean-focused finance.

nature-gov-041.title: SDG 13: climate action
nature-gov-041.text: Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, nations agreed to keep warming well under 2 °C. Their pledges would still lead to about 2.7 °C by 2100. Sustainable Development Goal 13, "Climate action," calls for urgent action to limit climate change and adapt to its impacts. Its five targets for 2030 include making societies more resilient to climate disasters and building climate measures into national policy. Target 13.a refers to developed countries' promise to mobilize $100 billion a year by 2020 for developing countries. One indicator simply counts the countries with national climate pledges and adaptation plans. COVID-19 cut 2020 emissions about 6% below projections, but the fall was only temporary. Critics say the goal overlooks climate migration as a way people adapt.

nature-gov-020.title: IPBES: the scientists' voice for biodiversity
nature-gov-020.text: In 2019, representatives of 132 member countries met in Paris and adopted the largest study yet of biodiversity and ecosystem services. It came from IPBES, an independent intergovernmental body that governments set up in 2012 to link biodiversity science to policy. A 2010 UN General Assembly resolution had asked UNEP to convene the meeting that created it. Its role resembles that of the IPCC for climate. Besides assessments, it also builds knowledge, skills and tools for policy-makers. Its members meet in plenaries every one to two years. A 2020 report found that preventing pandemics through conservation costs less than responding after outbreaks. In October 2022, IPBES and the IPCC shared the Gulbenkian Prize for Humanity. In January 2026 the United States announced it would withdraw.

nature-gov-055.title: The UN treaty against desertification
nature-gov-055.text: Desertification, in the treaty's words, is land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid regions, caused by climate swings and human activity. The UN Convention to Combat Desertification tackles it, and eases drought, through long-term national programs backed by international cooperation. It was adopted in Paris on 17 June 1994 and has been in force since December 1996. It is the only convention to grow directly out of Agenda 21, and the only binding international framework on desertification. It has 197 parties. Its key tools are National Action Programmes, drawn up with local communities. Its 2018–2030 framework aims for land degradation neutrality, no net loss of healthy land, and stronger drought resilience. At its COP16 meeting in Riyadh in December 2024, countries pledged more than US$12 billion.

nature-gov-043.title: Biodiversity action plans: a country's to-do list for nature
nature-gov-043.text: A national plan to protect biodiversity may cost up to 100 million pounds sterling, plus about ten percent of that every year to maintain. For poorer countries, that is a strain. A biodiversity action plan is a national or local program to protect and restore threatened species and habitats. The idea came from the 1992 Biodiversity Convention, which asked nations to build conservation strategies. A typical plan lists species or habitats, rates how threatened they are, sets targets, and lays out budgets, timelines and partners. Plans can center on species, habitats or farming. As of 2009, 191 countries had ratified the convention, but only some had full plans. Critics say many are paperwork, and almost all ignore fungi, invertebrates and micro-organisms. Some developing countries object that the plans put wildlife above food and industry.

nature-gov-030.title: SDG 15: life on land
nature-gov-030.text: Forests cover roughly 4 billion hectares, or 30.7 per cent of the world's land. About 93 percent are natural and 7 percent planted. Sustainable Development Goal 15, "Life on land," aims to protect, restore and sustainably use land ecosystems, manage forests, fight desertification and halt biodiversity loss. It has 12 targets for 2030, tracked by 14 indicators. They include ending deforestation, restoring degraded land, protecting habitats and sharing gene-based benefits fairly. Target 15.5 on threatened species is measured by the Red List Index. Target 15.9 asks countries to count nature's value in national planning and accounts. The trends point the wrong way. Deforestation is estimated to have risen by 12% from 2019 to 2020. As of 2023, low-income countries faced a funding gap of about $700 billion for protecting biodiversity.

nature-gov-057.title: World Heritage Sites: places that belong to everyone
nature-gov-057.text: World Heritage Sites cover less than 1% of the planet. Yet nearly three-quarters of bird species and two-thirds of mammals have been recorded in them. A World Heritage Site is a landmark or area protected under a UNESCO treaty for its outstanding cultural, historical or natural value to humanity. UNESCO adopted the World Heritage Convention on 16 November 1972. It took effect on 17 December 1975 and had 196 states as of November 2024. A site must have "outstanding universal value" and meet at least one of ten criteria, such as holding key habitats for biodiversity. Listing brings recognition, legal protection, possible money from the World Heritage Fund and often more tourists. Threatened sites can go on a danger list, and only three have ever been removed from the main list. Critics point to a lobbying industry chasing tourism returns, and costly bids that disadvantage poorer countries.

nature-gov-051.title: The Ramsar Convention: saving the world's wetlands
nature-gov-051.text: Every 2 February is World Wetlands Day. It marks the signing of a treaty at Ramsar, Iran, in 1971, for the conservation and wise use of wetlands of international importance. The Ramsar Convention, also called the Convention on Wetlands, took effect on 21 December 1975. To join, a country had to name at least one wetland and guarantee its protection. In February 2025 its list held 2,531 Ramsar sites covering over 2.6 million square kilometres. On paper that is a large estate. At home, though, countries often put the treaty into practice half-heartedly and inadequately.

nature-gov-017.title: The Aichi Targets: twenty goals that were missed
nature-gov-017.text: In October 2010, at a meeting in Nagoya, Japan, the parties to the Biodiversity Convention agreed 20 targets for the decade to 2020. These were the Aichi Biodiversity Targets, part of a strategic plan with five broad goals. Goal A went after the root causes of biodiversity loss by building nature into every part of government and society. Others aimed to cut direct pressures on nature, safeguard ecosystems, species and genetic diversity, and increase the benefits of ecosystem services. The convention later mapped how they overlapped with the 17 SDGs. Countries failed to meet them. The targets lacked clarity, were hard to measure, went unreported and had too little funding.

nature-gov-036.title: The Nagoya Protocol: paying for the genes you take
nature-gov-036.text: Taking a plant's genes from another country without permission is now illegal under the Nagoya Protocol. This 2010 add-on to the Biodiversity Convention carries out the treaty's third goal: fair sharing of the benefits from genetic resources. It was adopted on 29 October 2010 in Nagoya, Japan, and entered into force on 12 October 2014. By August 2025 it had 142 parties. Access needs prior informed consent and mutually agreed terms. Benefits may be money, such as royalties, or something else, such as shared research results. Traditional knowledge about genetic resources is covered too, and cannot be used without the holding communities' permission. Users must track resources after they leave a country, through checkpoints from research to sale. One gap remains. Genes from the high seas fall outside it, because it covers only national territory.

nature-gov-049.title: The High Seas Treaty: governing ocean no one owns
nature-gov-049.text: About two-thirds of the ocean lies beyond any nation's control, and until recently it was largely unregulated. The High Seas Treaty is a binding agreement under the Law of the Sea convention to conserve and sustainably use marine life in those areas. Its text was adopted on 19 June 2023. Morocco's ratification on 19 September 2025 brought the count to 60, and the treaty took effect on 17 January 2026. It covers four elements: marine genetic resources, tools such as marine protected areas, environmental impact assessments, and building countries' capacity. Benefits from marine genes, used in cosmetics and medicines, must be shared, though fish and fishing are excluded. High-seas protected areas can be adopted by consensus or a three-quarter majority and then bind all parties. Negotiators had to bridge two old ideas: freedom of the seas and the common heritage of humankind.

nature-gov-026.title: Conservation outside the fence: OECMs
nature-gov-026.text: Some of the best-kept nature on Earth sits outside any official reserve. Other effective area-based conservation measures, or OECMs, are such sites: governed and managed so that they conserve biodiversity in place over the long term. Unlike protected areas, they need not be set aside for conservation, but they must deliver it. The term first appeared in Aichi Target 11 in 2010. That target sought to conserve 17% of land and inland waters and 10% of coastal and marine areas by 2020. The convention formalized the definition in 2018, building on Canadian guidelines and IUCN advice. OECMs count toward Target 3 of the Global Biodiversity Framework. As of June 2026, 7,488 sites cover 1.31% of Earth's surface, about 1.1% on land and 0.21% at sea. They allow small-scale uses such as fishing and low-impact agroforestry. Locally managed marine areas are one form. They aim to be fairer than protected areas, which have displaced people.

nature-gov-014.title: What the SDGs would cost
nature-gov-014.text: In 2014, UNCTAD estimated that reaching the Sustainable Development Goals would cost US$2.5 trillion a year. A 2020 estimate put developing countries' financing gap at the same US$2.5 trillion a year before COVID-19, rising to US$4.2 trillion in 2020. The 2015 Addis Ababa Action Agenda is one UN process for raising the money. Private investment is seen as essential, and blended finance, which mixes public and private money, is designed to help.

openers.biodiversity-agreements-and-targets: In 2015 every member of the United Nations signed up to 17 shared goals, three of them about climate, oceans and land. Behind those goals stands a web of treaties: one to conserve the variety of life, one to fight desertification, one for the oceans, one for places of outstanding value to humanity. Many of them work by protecting places, limiting what people may take from them. Others decide who may use the genes of plants, animals and microbes, and who gets paid when they do. This chapter follows those agreements and targets, and asks how well they have worked.
